problem: Earlier cross-embodiment robot policies (RT-X, Octo, GNM/ViNT, Yang et al. 2024) either train on robots that share one observation and action format, or manually align actions across embodiments (e.g., navigation waypoints to wrist-camera arm motion). They therefore cannot jointly control robots whose sensors and actuators are disjoint, such as bimanual 14-DoF arms, 12-joint quadrupeds and 2D-waypoint ground or aerial navigators.
motivation: Each robot and task usually has only a small dataset, while pooling multi-robot data could give broader generalization and remove per-robot architecture engineering. The paper's observation is that a sequence-model transformer can serialize any set of cameras and proprioception. Adding embodiment-specific readout tokens and heads then lets it output actions of any dimension and chunk length without aligning action spaces.
key_idea: CrossFormer is a single 130M-parameter causal transformer trained on 20 embodiments. It tokenizes whatever observations each robot has, places embodiment-specific action-readout token groups at fixed positions in the context, and decodes them with separate per-action-type L1 regression heads that output action chunks, so no observation or action alignment is needed.
insight: Heterogeneous data can be absorbed without negative transfer. Averaged over all real-robot evaluations, CrossFormer scores 0.73 versus 0.68 (Table; the text says 67%) for the same architecture trained only on the target robot's data. It also beats the best per-robot prior methods (0.51) and outperforms Yang et al.'s manually aligned cross-embodiment policy by about 3x, including on LoCoBot navigation. Per the authors, the gains come from keeping observation and readout token groups in fixed context slots, which makes the embodiment implicit in the readout positional embeddings, and from per-embodiment chunk sizes. However, the authors say the results do not yet show significant positive transfer across embodiments. There is no formal ablation table; they only note that navigation needed 5 timesteps of history, which did not hurt the other embodiments.
method: Observation tokenization: each image view goes through a ResNet-26 (ImageNet-initialized) whose flattened feature map is projected to 512-d tokens. Proprioception is linearly projected. Encoders are shared per view type (4 encoders: workspace, navigation egocentric, 2 wrist). Missing observations are masked but keep fixed slots.

Task conditioning: a language instruction is fused via FiLM with the image encoder, or a goal image is channel-stacked with the current image. Language or goal is randomly masked during training, with hindsight goal relabeling from uniformly sampled future frames.

Block-wise causal transformer backbone: 12 layers, 8 heads, 512-d embeddings, MLP dimension 2048. Context is 2135 tokens covering 5 timesteps, and observation tokens attend only to the same or earlier timesteps.
Action readout tokens (following Octo): N readout tokens are inserted per timestep, where N equals the action chunk size of that embodiment. They attend only to prior observation tokens.

Four action heads with L1 regression: single-arm 7-D delta end-effector pose (chunk 4, 5–15 Hz); navigation 2-D relative waypoints (chunk 4, 4 Hz); bimanual 14-D joint positions (chunk 100, 20 Hz); quadruped 12-D joint positions (chunk 1, 20 Hz).

Data mixture: OXE single-arm subset (Octo mix), DROID, BridgeData, GNM (60 h of navigation), ALOHA-multi-task (7K trajectories), Go1-walk (25 min of rollouts from an RL expert) and Franka-tabletop (200 trajectories). Target datasets are up-weighted with hand-picked sampling weights, and training runs 300K steps at batch size 512 on a TPU v5e-256.

Navigation deployment: the navigation head is combined with ViNT's graph planner and distance function over a teleoperated topological map of goal images. At each step the planner picks the most immediate subgoal image to condition the policy.

setting.backbone: CrossFormer: 12-layer causal transformer + ResNet-26 image encoders (ImageNet init) + 4 linear action heads, trained end-to-end (imitation learning)
setting.training_data: Large multi-embodiment mixture of 20 embodiments; the trajectory count is a macro (\ntrajs) not expanded in the source text. It combines the OXE single-arm subset (Octo mix), DROID, Bridge, GNM (60 h of navigation), ALOHA-multi-task (7K trajectories, collected for this paper), Go1-walk (25 min of RL-expert rollouts) and Franka-tabletop (200 trajectories), with up-weighted target datasets.
setting.observation: Varies by embodiment. Navigation: egocentric monocular RGB with 5-step history plus goal image. Manipulation: third-person and/or wrist RGB plus optional joint proprioception. Quadruped: 59-D proprioception only. Tasks are given as a language instruction or goal image.
setting.action_space: Embodiment-specific. Navigation: 2-D relative waypoints (chunk of 4, 4 Hz; fixed altitude on the quadcopter). Single arm: 7-D delta end-effector + gripper. Bimanual: 14-D joint positions (chunk 100). Quadruped: 12-D joint positions.
setting.simulator: real world only (Go1 data generated by an RL expert trained in simulation)
setting.privileged: Navigation uses a pre-collected (teleoperated) topological map of goal images plus ViNT's graph planner and distance function to select subgoals (pre-exploration). Manipulation goal images are taken after arranging the scene.

numbers_note: No standard simulated navigation benchmark is used; all results are small real-world trials (only 2 trials per LoCoBot skill, 3 for Tello). The comparison with Yang et al. 2024 is shown only in a figure (described as '3x overall'; Yang et al. score 0 on WidowX), and those numbers are not extractable. The main-text Figure bar chart duplicates the appendix table. Inconsistencies: the single-robot baseline average is 67% in the text but 0.68 in the table, and training time is 47 hours in the main text but 80 hours in the appendix. The trajectory-count macro (\ntrajs) is not expanded in the source.
results: Across 6 real-world embodiment settings, the single CrossFormer policy averages 0.73 success, versus 0.68 for the same architecture trained only on target-robot data and 0.51 for the best per-robot prior methods (Octo, OpenVLA, ACT, ViNT). On LoCoBot navigation it reaches 0.95/0.95/0.88 on obstacle avoidance, cornering and sharp cornering, against ViNT's 0.30/0.85/0.30. It transfers zero-shot to a Tello quadcopter (0.82 vs 0.68 for ViNT). It outperforms Yang et al.'s action-aligned cross-embodiment policy by about 3x on navigation and WidowX manipulation.
limitations: No significant positive transfer across embodiments: the method mainly avoids negative transfer, and its gains over the single-robot baseline are small and based on very few real trials.

Relies on hand-picked dataset sampling weights. Navigation also depends on a teleoperated topological goal-image map plus ViNT's planner, and is limited to 2-D waypoints (fixed altitude for the drone).
Inference latency of larger models may prevent controlling high-frequency embodiments as the model scales.
